title: The Journey of a Raindrop
subtitle: Clouds, rivers, oceans, ice, and the water that never stops moving
subject: Earth

p: Fill a glass of water and look at it. Some of those drops were once inside a dinosaur. Some fell as snow on a woolly mammoth. Some sat in the ocean for thousands of years before a cloud lifted them out.

Earth has had almost the same water for about 4 billion years. It does not get used up. It just keeps moving: up into the sky, down as rain, along rivers, into the sea, and up again. This book follows one raindrop around that endless loop.
pages.cap: Up, across, down, and around again. The water cycle never stops.
pages.fact: Did you know? Earth holds about 1.4 billion cubic kilometres of water. A cubic kilometre is a block 1 km on each side.

p: Imagine all the water on Earth poured into 100 bottles. About 97 of them would be salty ocean. Two more would be frozen in glaciers and ice sheets, mostly in Antarctica and Greenland. Less than one bottle would be fresh water you could drink.

Most of that last bottle is hidden underground, soaked into rock and soil. All the rivers and lakes in the world together would be just a few drops at the bottom. Fresh, liquid, easy-to-reach water is rare. That is why it is precious.

v.title: Out of 100 bottles of Earth's water

pages.cap: Almost all of Earth's water is too salty or too frozen to drink.
pages.fact: Did you know? The Great Lakes hold about one fifth of all the liquid fresh water on the surface of the Earth.

p: Every drop of water is made of tiny pieces called molecules. One water molecule is two hydrogen atoms stuck to one oxygen atom. Scientists write it as H2O. Molecules are so small that a single drop holds more than a billion trillion of them.

Water molecules are a little sticky. They cling to each other, which is why drops are round, why water climbs up a paper towel, and why some insects can walk on a pond. Water is the only common thing on Earth that is naturally found as a solid, a liquid and a gas.
pages.cap: One oxygen atom, two hydrogen atoms: H2O.
pages.fact: Did you know? Water molecules are so sticky that a water strider's six feet can rest on a pond without breaking the surface.

pages.h: A cloud can weigh as much as 100 elephants
p: A fluffy white cumulus cloud 1 km across holds about 500 tonnes of water. It floats because that water is spread out as droplets smaller than dust, and the warm air under it keeps pushing up.

pages.h: Step one: up into the air
p: Our raindrop starts in the ocean. The Sun warms the surface. Some molecules at the top get enough energy to break free and float up as water vapour, an invisible gas. This is evaporation. It happens from oceans, lakes, puddles, wet clothes and even your skin.

You cannot see water vapour. Steam from a kettle is actually tiny droplets that have already cooled. Every day, the Sun lifts about 1,400 cubic kilometres of water into the sky. That is enough to cover all of Canada 14 cm deep.
pages.cap: Heat gives molecules the energy to escape as a gas.
pages.fact: Did you know? Plants evaporate water too. A large tree can push more than 300 L of water out through its leaves on one hot summer day.

pages.q: Out of every 100 bottles of water on Earth, about how many are salty ocean?
pages.why: About 97 percent of Earth's water is in the oceans. Only a tiny slice is fresh and easy to reach.

p: Warm air rises. As it climbs, it cools, about 1 degree Celsius for every 100 m. Cold air cannot hold as much vapour. So the vapour turns back into tiny liquid droplets. That is condensation, the same thing that happens on the outside of a cold glass.

The droplets need something to form on: a speck of dust, salt from sea spray, or smoke. Billions of these droplets, each about 0.02 mm across, together make a cloud. Our raindrop is now one of them, floating 2 km above the sea.
pages.cap: Vapour cools and gathers into liquid droplets around specks of dust.
pages.fact: Did you know? Fog is just a cloud that touches the ground. Walk through fog and you are walking through a cloud.

p: A cloud droplet is far too light to fall. It has to grow. Droplets bump into each other and join. It takes about a million cloud droplets to make one raindrop big enough to fall.

A raindrop is not shaped like a teardrop. Small ones are round balls. Bigger ones flatten on the bottom like a hamburger bun as they push through the air. Most are 1 to 4 mm across and fall at about 15 to 30 km per hour. A drop wider than 5 mm breaks apart in the wind.
pages.cap: Falling drops bend sunlight into a rainbow.
pages.fact: Did you know? In cold clouds, drops freeze into snowflakes. Every snowflake has six sides, because of the way water molecules lock together.

pages.h: Try it: a water cycle in a bag
p: Watch the whole cycle happen on your window.
steps: Draw a sun and a cloud on a clear zip bag with a marker.
Pour in about 50 mL of water, a quarter cup, and add a drop of blue food colouring.
Seal the bag and tape it to a sunny window.
Check every hour. Droplets will form near the top, then slide down like rain.
Try a second bag on a shady window. Which one makes more rain?
pages.cap: Sun heats the water, vapour rises, droplets gather, rain falls. All in one bag.
pages.safe: Ask before taping to a window, and wipe up any drips.

p: If the air is cold enough, our raindrop falls as snow. Snow is fluffy because every flake is mostly air. About 10 cm of fresh snow melts down to only 1 cm of water.

Water is strange when it freezes. Almost everything shrinks when it gets cold. Water grows. Ice takes up about 9 percent more space than the water it came from, which is why a frozen bottle can crack and why ice floats. If ice sank, lakes would freeze from the bottom up and fish could not survive the winter.
pages.cap: Frozen water molecules lock into a loose six-sided pattern with gaps in it.
pages.fact: Did you know? Canada's record for the most snow in one winter is about 24 m, measured on Mount Copeland in British Columbia in 1971 to 1972.

p: About 7 out of every 10 litres of the world's fresh water is locked in ice. The Antarctic ice sheet is up to 4.8 km thick, thick enough to bury almost 9 CN Towers stacked on top of each other. Snow that fell there has been squeezed into ice for ages.

Scientists drill out long cores of this ice. Bubbles trapped inside hold tiny samples of ancient air. The oldest ice ever drilled, pulled up in 2025, is more than 1.2 million years old. If all the ice on Earth melted, the sea would rise about 70 m.
pages.cap: Nine tenths of an iceberg hides under the water.
pages.fact: Did you know? The largest iceberg ever measured was about 11,000 square kilometres, nearly twice the size of Prince Edward Island.

pages.q: Why does ice float on water?
opts: Ice is lighter because it has air in it
Water takes up more space when it freezes
pages.why: When water freezes, its molecules lock into a pattern with gaps, so ice takes up about 9 percent more space than the same water. More space for the same weight means it floats.

p: Our raindrop lands on a hillside. It joins other drops, trickles into a stream, and the stream joins a river. Rivers always run downhill, carving valleys over millions of years.

The longest river in Canada is the Mackenzie, flowing 4,241 km north to the Arctic Ocean. The world's biggest river is the Amazon in South America. It carries about one fifth of all the river water on Earth, more than the next seven biggest rivers put together. Scientists still argue whether the Nile or the Amazon is longer. Both are about 6,500 km.
pages.cap: Rain soaks through soil and rock, then seeps out into streams.
pages.fact: Did you know? The Amazon is so wide that in many places you cannot see across it: about 10 km in the dry season, and far more when it floods.

p: Not every drop runs off into a river. Much of the rain soaks straight into the ground. It trickles down through soil and tiny cracks in rock until it reaches a layer that is already full. This underground water is called groundwater.

There is about 100 times more fresh water underground than in all the rivers and lakes on Earth. Wells reach down to it. About one in four Canadians drinks groundwater. Some of it has been underground for 10,000 years, since the last ice age.
pages.cap: Water seeps into rock the way it seeps into a sugar cube.
pages.fact: Did you know? Some springs in the Rocky Mountains pour out water that fell as rain or snow before the pyramids were built.

p: Our raindrop reaches the ocean at last. The ocean is enormous. It covers 71 percent of the planet and its average depth is 3.7 km. The deepest spot, the Challenger Deep near Guam, is 10,935 m down. Mount Everest could sit on the bottom and still have 2 km of water above it.

Every litre of seawater holds about 35 g of salt, about six teaspoons. The salt came from rocks, washed in by rivers for billions of years. Rivers carry the salt in, but when the water evaporates, the salt stays behind.
pages.cap: In the deep sea, no sunlight reaches, and the pressure is crushing.
pages.fact: Did you know? If all the salt in the ocean were spread over the land, it would make a layer 150 m deep.

pages.h: One drop can spend 3,000 years in the ocean
p: Water moves fast through the sky, about 9 days from evaporating to falling. In the sea it can drift for thousands of years. In Antarctic ice, a snowflake might stay frozen for a million. The journey is the same loop, but the stops are very different lengths.

The sea is never still. Huge currents flow through it like rivers inside the ocean. The Gulf Stream carries warm water from near Mexico across the Atlantic, which is why northern Europe is milder than Canada at the same distance from the North Pole.

Tides lift the whole ocean twice a day, pulled by the Moon's gravity. In the Bay of Fundy, between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, the water rises and falls by up to 16 m, the highest tide on Earth. That is the height of a five-storey building, twice a day, every day.
pages.cap: Sailors have used currents and tides for thousands of years.
pages.fact: Did you know? The Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth, about 4 cm a year, so tides were stronger when dinosaurs lived.

pages.q: Where is most of the world's fresh water?
opts: Frozen in ice sheets and glaciers
pages.why: About 70 percent of fresh water is frozen, mostly in Antarctica and Greenland. Rivers and lakes hold only a tiny fraction.

p: Oceans soak up heat from the Sun and carry it around the planet. Water vapour rising from warm seas feeds storms. A hurricane is a giant engine powered by evaporating ocean water, and it can pour down more than 500 mm of rain in a day, as much as some cities get in a year.

Water also cools things. Sweat evaporating off your skin takes heat with it. That is why you feel cooler when you are wet and a breeze blows. Cities near big lakes have milder winters and cooler summers for the same reason.
pages.cap: A storm is water vapour giving back the Sun's energy, all at once.
pages.fact: Did you know? The wettest place on Earth, Mawsynram in India, gets about 11,870 mm of rain a year. Vancouver gets about 1,200 mm.

p: About 6 out of every 10 kg of you is water. Your brain is about three quarters water. Your blood is mostly water. Water carries food to your cells, carries waste away, keeps you cool and cushions your joints.

You lose about 1.5 L a day through breath, sweat and pee, so you have to keep topping up. A child your age needs about 1.5 L a day from drinks and food. A person can live for weeks without food but only about 3 days without water. Fruit helps: a watermelon is 92 percent water.
pages.cap: Every cell in your body is a tiny bag of mostly water.
pages.fact: Did you know? A jellyfish is about 95 percent water. Take the water away and almost nothing is left.

p: Life on Earth started in water, about 3.8 billion years ago, as tiny single cells in the sea. For most of Earth's history, water was the only place anything lived. Land stayed almost empty for more than 3 billion years.

Water is special because so many things dissolve in it. Salt, sugar, oxygen and minerals all float around inside it, ready for living things to use. Scientists looking for life on other planets look for water first. Mars once had rivers and lakes, and moons of Jupiter and Saturn hide whole oceans under their ice.
pages.cap: The first living cells divided in ancient seas.
pages.fact: Did you know? Jupiter's moon Europa may hold twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans.

pages.h: Try it: catch and measure the rain
p: Be a weather scientist with a jar and a ruler.
steps: Find a straight-sided jar or can. Put it outside in an open spot, away from trees and walls.
After it rains, use a ruler to measure how deep the water is in millimetres.
Write the number down with the date. Empty the jar.
Keep going for a month. Add up your numbers.
Compare with the weather report. Was your jar close?
pages.cap: Weather stations measure rain in exactly this way, with a straight-sided container.
pages.safe: Pick a spot where the jar cannot be knocked over or blown away.

p: Water does more than fill glasses. It grows nearly all our food. It makes about 6 out of every 10 units of Canada's electricity, by spinning turbines in dams. It carries ships, cools factories and puts out fires.

An average Canadian uses about 220 L of water at home every day. A five-minute shower uses about 45 L. One toilet flush uses about 6 L in a new toilet, but 13 L in an old one. Growing the wheat and raising the cow for a single hamburger takes around 2,000 L.
pages.cap: Every light in a city, and every tap, depends on moving water.
pages.fact: Did you know? A dripping tap, one drop per second, wastes about 20 L a day and 7,000 L a year.

pages.q: About how long does a drop of water usually spend in the air, from evaporating to falling as rain?
pages.why: On average, water stays in the atmosphere about 9 days before it falls again. The ocean and ice hold water for much, much longer.

p: Turn a tap in Canada and clean water comes out. Around the world, about 2 billion people do not have safe drinking water at home. Many walk long distances every day to fetch it, often more than 5 km, carrying 20 kg jugs on their heads and backs. Most of the carriers are women and girls.

Dirty water spreads diseases. Clean water, wells and simple filters save lives. Even in Canada, some communities, many of them First Nations, have had to boil their water for years. Water is not just science. It is fairness.
pages.cap: Clean water should reach every child in the world.
pages.fact: Did you know? A simple sand and gravel filter can clean dirty river water enough to drink.

p: Whatever we pour down a drain or drop in a river rides the water cycle too. Oil, soap, fertilizer and plastic all end up in streams and finally the sea. Tiny plastic pieces have now been found in rain, in snow in the Arctic and in the deepest ocean trench.

The good news is that water cleans itself if we give it a chance. Wetlands filter it. Soil filters it. Evaporation leaves dirt behind. Your job is simple: use less, waste nothing, and keep rubbish out of the water. The raindrop you save today will be back.
pages.cap: A healthy reef needs clean water flowing in from the land.
pages.fact: Did you know? A single wetland the size of a soccer field can filter the dirty water from a whole neighbourhood.

p: Our raindrop evaporated from the sea, floated as a cloud, fell as rain, ran through a river, hid underground, and came back to the ocean. It might do that journey a thousand more times before you grow up.

Right now, somewhere, a drop that was once in your glass is rising from a lake. Another is a snowflake landing on a mountain. Another is in the blood of a whale. The water cycle has no start and no end. It is the oldest, biggest and most patient machine on Earth, and you are part of it.
pages.cap: The same water, around and around, for 4 billion years.
pages.fact: Did you know? Your next breath out contains water that will be rain somewhere within about two weeks.

items: water cycle
The endless loop of water moving between sea, sky and land.
evaporation
When liquid water turns into an invisible gas called water vapour.
condensation
When water vapour cools and turns back into liquid droplets.
precipitation
Any water falling from the sky: rain, snow, sleet or hail.
molecule
The smallest piece of water, made of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
groundwater
Fresh water hidden in soil and rock under the ground.
glacier
A huge, slow-moving river of ice.
current
A river of water flowing inside the ocean.
tide
The rise and fall of the sea, pulled by the Moon.
dissolve
When something mixes into water so completely that it seems to disappear.

qs: If you could follow one raindrop for a year, where would you hope it would go?
Everyone on Earth shares the same water. What should we do when one country's river flows into another country?
Water is free from the sky but costs money from a tap. Why do you think that is?
